fields.title: Praying Hyde (For Teens)
fields.description: In the villages of the Punjab they called him “the man who never sleeps.” John Hyde was a shy, slightly deaf American missionary who spent ten slow years in India before his prayers, his tears and his love for the poorest people around him made him known around the world as Praying Hyde. This teen edition tells his true story straight: the proud young man who crumpled a letter, the sin he couldn't preach past, the colleagues who misunderstood him, the drunk he never gave up on, the body he wore out, and the famous stories about him checked against the records.

qa.question: Who was John Hyde?
qa.answer: An American Presbyterian missionary, born in Illinois in 1865, who worked in the villages of the Punjab in British India from 1892 to 1911, around Ferozepore and later the Moga district. He helped lead the prayer at the Sialkot conventions, the people called him “the man who never sleeps,” and he died in Northampton, Massachusetts, in 1912.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how proud and ambitious he was as a young man, how he struggled with a sin he never named, how his first ten years in India bore little fruit, and how colleagues disapproved of him. It also says plainly that his way of praying, with little food or sleep, wore down his health and should not be copied.

qa.question: What does “Father, give me these souls or I die” mean?
qa.answer: It was Hyde's cry in prayer during the summer of 1908, heard by friends as he pleaded for the people of his district. It echoes Rachel's cry for children in Genesis: he longed for people to come to Christ the way a childless parent longs for a child.

qa.question: Did he really win a soul a day, then four a day?
qa.answer: The exact numbers come from one memoir written by friends more than ten years later, and no mission report yet found confirms them. The records do show baptisms rising for five years in his Moga district, 685 in 1910, and Hyde himself wrote that his team had seen over a thousand in two years. The real story is smaller than the legend, and still remarkable.

qa.question: Did prayer really move his heart to the other side of his chest?
qa.answer: That claim rests on a friend's later memory of one doctor's remark in Calcutta in 1910. The doctor did not know the cause, and a heart on the right side has known medical explanations. Hyde certainly wore his body down, but the miracle is left unclaimed.

qa.question: How did he treat people who wronged him?
qa.answer: With remarkable patience. He said colleagues who disapproved of him simply did not understand and never meant to be unkind. He kept taking back a young man who stole his clothes for drink, and he called unfair treatment “my cross” rather than defending himself.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of John Hyde, which draws on two small books of memories written by his friends in 1923 and checks them against mission reports, church magazines and an obituary by a fellow missionary. When a story rests only on one friend's memory, this edition says so.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That God works through weakness and slow years; that being honest about your own sin matters more than looking good; that the hidden work of praying for others is real work; and that rest, food and sleep are gifts, so follow his spirit, not his exhausting form.

fields.title: Thrust Out Laborers
fields.body_html:
“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth laborers into his harvest.” — Matthew 9:38 (ASV)

John Nelson Hyde was born on 9 November 1865 at Carrollton, Illinois, the year the American Civil War ended. He grew up as one of six children in a minister's home. His father, Smith Harris Hyde, was pastor of the Presbyterian church in Carthage, a small prairie town in western Illinois, for seventeen years. His mother was remembered as “sweet-spirited, gentle, music-loving, Christ-like.” Years later John told a friend she had been the best singer he had ever heard, and “such a holy woman.”

It was an ordinary Christian home: a family altar, a praying father, a mother who sang. But one thing stood out. A young minister who often ate at the Hydes' table heard Dr. Hyde pray the same prayer again and again, at home with his children listening and from the pulpit on Sundays. It was the command of Jesus at the top of this chapter. In the older English that minister remembered, he asked the Lord to “thrust out laborers” into his harvest. Most parents quietly add “but not mine” to that prayer. Smith Hyde didn't. He “magnified his office and rejoiced to give his sons up to a life of hardship and trial.”

John graduated from Carthage College in 1887, and years later he admitted what had been going on inside him. He had decided to be a missionary, but a great one. “I wanted to shine as a great missionary,” he told a friend. He was “a little proud of the 'B.A.' after my name.” And he was honest about it: “I loved the Lord and I wanted to serve Him, but 'self' was at the foundation of my ambition.”

In 1889 he went to McCormick Theological Seminary in Chicago. His older brother Edmund followed him there. Edmund had joined the Student Volunteers, college students who pledged to serve overseas if God allowed. One summer he went to do mission work in Montana and caught a fever. Too ill to travel safely, he was put on a train home with his ticket and instructions pinned to his coat. He reached home delirious and died a few days later, in August 1891. He was about twenty-eight. John “was deeply impressed by his brother's death,” and wondered “if it were not God's will for him to step into the gap.”

He didn't decide in a rush of grief. He carried the question for most of a year. Then, late one Saturday night in his final year, he went to a classmate's room and asked for all the arguments for and against going abroad. The classmate refused. Arguments weren't what he needed, he said. He should go to his own room, get on his knees, and stay there till the question was settled. John went. The next morning at chapel he found his friend and said, “It is settled.” His friend remembered that “his shining face was enough to show which way the decision had been made.”

On 15 October 1892, newly ordained, he sailed from New York for the Punjab in north-west India. He was twenty-six. A father's prayer had been answered through his own son.

Notice two things. First, the decision you keep reopening with one more argument may need time on your knees more than another opinion. Second, John went with mixed motives: real love for God, and a big wish to be admired. That is normal. God doesn't wait until your motives are pure before he sends you. He often purifies them on the way, if you let him.

One thing to do this week: write down the one question about your future that you keep going round in circles about. Instead of asking for one more opinion, spend ten quiet minutes with it in prayer, with your phone in another room, and tell God honestly that you are willing to hear his answer, whatever it is.

study_questions.question: What prayer did John Hyde's father pray again and again?
study_questions.answer: Jesus' prayer that the Lord of the harvest would send out labourers into his harvest. He prayed it with his own children listening, and was glad to give his sons to hard work for God.

study_questions.question: How did John finally settle whether to become a missionary?
study_questions.answer: A classmate refused to give him more arguments and told him to kneel in his room until the question was settled. The next morning John said, “It is settled.”

study_questions.question: What did John later admit about his motives as a young man?
study_questions.answer: That he wanted to shine as a great missionary and was proud of his degree. He loved the Lord, but “self” was at the foundation of his ambition.

fields.title: The Crumpled Letter
fields.body_html:
“If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” — Luke 11:13 (ASV)

When John Hyde went aboard his steamer in New York, a letter was waiting for him. It was from a friend of his father's, an older Christian who had longed to be a missionary himself but had never been allowed to go. “The words were not many,” Hyde said years later, “but the purport of them was this: 'I shall not cease praying for you, dear John, until you are filled with the Holy Spirit.'”

Hyde was furious. He told a close friend exactly how he reacted:

“My pride was touched, and I felt exceedingly angry and crushed the letter and threw it into a corner of the cabin and went up on deck in a very angry spirit. The idea of implying that I was not filled with the Spirit!”

He was going out as a missionary. Who was this man to suggest he wasn't ready? He paced the deck with “a battle raging within.” But he loved the man who wrote the letter, and he knew the holy life he lived. Deep down, Hyde admitted, “there was a conviction that he was right and that I was not fit to be a missionary.” So he went back to his cabin, got down on his knees to hunt for the crumpled letter, smoothed it out, and read it again. And then again.

For two or three days he fought it, “until I felt perfectly miserable.” Then, “in a kind of despair,” he asked the Lord to fill him with the Holy Spirit, “and the moment I did this the whole atmosphere seemed to clear up. I began to see myself, and what a selfish ambition I had.”

It was a struggle almost to the end of the voyage. But before the ship reached port he had made up his mind. He told the Lord he was willing even to fail his language exams in India. He was willing to be a missionary “working quietly out of sight.” He would do anything and be anything, “but the Holy Spirit I would have at any cost.”

There are two tellings of this story. In one he throws the letter on the deck; in the other, into a corner of the cabin. Details like that drift when a story is told years apart. Both agree on what matters: a hard word from someone who loved him, a proud reaction, and then a change of heart. One of Hyde's friends understood that the letter-writer was the minister who later wrote a short book about Hyde. That may be true, but nobody can be certain, so treat it as a possibility.

The young man who wanted to shine asked instead to be hidden. As it turned out, that was almost a description of the rest of his life.

Everybody gets a letter like that sooner or later: a comment from a parent, a coach, a youth leader or a friend that stings because part of it is true. Pride crumples it up. Grace goes back to look for it. Not every criticism comes from God, and some of it deserves the bin. But some of it is what Proverbs calls the “wounds of a friend.” And notice how simple Jesus makes the answer to feeling spiritually empty. You ask. The Father gives the Holy Spirit “to them that ask him.”

One thing to do this week: think of a criticism you brushed off recently. Go back and smooth it out: write it down and ask honestly whether any part of it is true. If it is, thank the person who said it, and ask God for the help you actually need.

study_questions.question: What did the letter on the ship say?
study_questions.answer: Its writer, a friend of Hyde's father, promised that he would not stop praying for John until he was filled with the Holy Spirit.

study_questions.question: How did Hyde first react, and what changed his mind?
study_questions.answer: He crumpled the letter in anger and threw it away. Deep down he knew the writer was right, so he went back on his knees, found it, and read it again until he asked God to fill him.

study_questions.question: What was Hyde willing to give up by the end of the voyage?
study_questions.answer: Even passing his language exams and being noticed. He would be a missionary working quietly out of sight, as long as he had the Holy Spirit.

fields.title: A Question in the Street
fields.body_html:
“Therefore let us also, seeing we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us” — Hebrews 12:1 (ASV)

Hyde reached the Punjab at the end of 1892. It was a land of wheat fields, canal villages and mud-walled towns, now divided between Pakistan and north-west India. He spoke neither of the languages he would need, Urdu and Punjabi. In his first few days an older missionary took him to an open-air meeting in the town. Hyde couldn't understand a word, but someone told him the subject: Jesus Christ, the real Saviour from sin.

When it was over, a respectable-looking man in the crowd who spoke good English stepped forward with a question for the preacher. Had he himself been saved from sin in the way he was describing?

We don't know how the older missionary answered. The story isn't about him. It's about the young man standing silently beside him, because the question went straight into Hyde's own heart. “If the question had been asked me,” he said later, “I would have had to confess that Christ had not fully saved me, because I knew that there was a sin in my life which had not been taken away.”

He never said what the sin was, and it's wise not to guess. He used the words of Hebrews, “the sin that so easily beset me.” It was one familiar failure that had followed him all the way from America. Leaving it unnamed is a kind of mercy, because it turns the story into a mirror. Almost everyone who reads it thinks of their own.

Hyde went back to his room, shut the door, and had it out with God:

“I told the Lord that it must be one of two things. Either He must give me victory over all my sins, and especially over the sin that so easily beset me, or I must return to America and seek there for some other work. I said that I could not stand up to preach the Gospel until I could testify of its power in my own life.”

That wasn't bargaining. It was a refusal to live a double life, preaching a Saviour from sin while quietly keeping the sin. He stayed in his room “for some time.” Then, he said, “The Lord assured me that He was able and willing to deliver me from all sin, that He had planned work for me in India. He did deliver me and I have not had a doubt of this since.” The friend who heard him tell it never forgot “that inexpressibly sad look when he spoke of his sin, and that wonderful smile of his when he referred to the faithfulness of Christ.”

It was a real beginning, not the end of the fight. Twelve years later Hyde was still telling other men about “some of the desperate conflicts that he had had with sin and how God had given him victory.” Freedom from a sin's rule is the start of a road.

Maybe there's one thing in your life you've half made peace with. It knows your tired hours and your weak places. Hyde's way is costly but simple: bring it to God as a question of honesty, and refuse to go on living divided. “Sin shall not have dominion over you” is not a promise that you'll never be tempted. It's a promise about who is in charge. And God's help often comes through people, so don't try to fight it completely alone.

One thing to do this week: name your own “besetting sin” to God this week, in plain words, when you're alone. Then tell one trusted, mature Christian about it (a parent, a pastor, a youth leader) and ask them to pray for you.

study_questions.question: What question did the man in the crowd ask?
study_questions.answer: Whether the missionary preaching about Christ as the Saviour from sin had himself been saved from sin in that way.

study_questions.question: Why did the question shake Hyde so much?
study_questions.answer: Because he knew there was a sin in his life that had not been taken away, and he could not honestly preach a Saviour who had not delivered him.

study_questions.question: Was Hyde's victory that day the end of his struggle with sin?
study_questions.answer: No. It was a real beginning. Twelve years later he was still speaking about his desperate conflicts with sin and how God had given him victory.

fields.title: Slow of Speech
fields.body_html:
“And Jehovah said unto him, Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh a man dumb, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? is it not I, Jehovah? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.” — Exodus 4:11-12 (ASV)

If Hyde's story were a legend, he would step off the ship and win the Punjab. He didn't. “At the first,” one early account admits, “John Hyde was not a remarkable missionary.” A colleague who wrote his obituary was blunter. Hyde's first ten years in India “were marked by steady, patient, but not especially fruitful service.”

Part of the reason was Hyde himself. He was hard of hearing, and it got worse over the years; near the end of his life he could rarely hear anything in church. People remembered that “when a question or a remark was directed to him he seemed not to hear, or if he heard he seemed a long time in framing a reply.” His closest friend said Hyde “was not naturally a bright and happy man. On the contrary he was in himself inclined to be morose, retiring, shy and silent.” The one thing everybody noticed was his “wonderful pair of blue eyes.” Picture it: a shy, slightly deaf young man, sent to learn two languages and preach in them to crowds.

Then he got into trouble. New missionaries were supposed to give their first years mainly to language study. Hyde neglected it for Bible study, and the mission committee told him off. His reply was “First things first.” He had come to teach the Bible, he argued, so he needed to know it. The committee had a fair point. A missionary who can't speak the language can't reach anyone. But Hyde didn't drop his language study altogether. He just wouldn't let it crowd out the Scriptures.

For years it looked as if he would never speak well. Then, his colleague wrote, “the baptism of the Spirit and the fire of love loosed his tongue and gave him free utterance.” In the end he preached in Urdu, Punjabi and English. Urdu speakers said he “spoke the language well, if anything a little highflown, using the book-language more than the colloquial.” That is exactly what you'd expect from a man who had learned his Urdu with an Urdu Bible in his hands.

The slow years cost him something else: his colleagues' approval. Many of them didn't like how much time he spent praying. Some thought him impractical, and it was true that he “had not the gifts of an organizer.” Years later a friend asked whether he had known that they disapproved. Hyde smiled: “Oh, yes, I knew it, but they did not understand me, that was all, they never intended to be unkind.” His friend added, “There was not one atom of bitterness as far as I could see.”

In 1901 Hyde went home to America on leave, partly for his health. In September 1902 he sailed back to India as he had left it: faithful, quiet, misunderstood, and with little to show. Nothing in the records of that year suggests the next ten years would be any different. They were.

When Moses complained that he was slow of speech, God didn't deny the problem. He said that he had made Moses' mouth, and promised to be with it. Hyde stayed deaf to the end. God didn't take the weakness away; he worked through it. If you're shy, or you struggle with something that seems to disqualify you, it isn't news to God. And if you've been faithful a long time with not much to show for it, those years may be the soil that everything else grows in.

One thing to do this week: the next time someone misunderstands or criticises you, try reading them the way Hyde read his colleagues: “they did not understand me, that was all, they never intended to be unkind.” Assume the best before you answer, and see what it does to your reply.

study_questions.answer: Without bitterness. He said they did not understand him and never intended to be unkind.

fields.title: Love Won Him Victories
fields.body_html:
“but God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might put to shame them that are wise; and God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong;” — 1 Corinthians 1:27 (ASV)

To understand Hyde, you have to understand the Punjab. It was a farming province of British India named after its five rivers. Its people were Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs, with very few Christians, and village life was ordered by caste. At the very bottom were landless labourers and sweepers then called Chuhras, a name used with contempt and today regarded as a slur. People of higher caste would not eat with them, touch them, or take water from their hands.

Around 1873 a man from that community named Ditt was baptized. He was a small, quiet man, lame in one leg, who made a thin living buying and selling hides. Instead of moving into the mission compound, as converts often did, he went home. His relatives were furious. His sister-in-law cursed him: “One of your legs is broken already; so may it be with the other.” Ditt answered, “Very well, my brethren; if it pleases you, you may oppose me and load me with reproaches and abuse; but your opposition will never induce me to deny Christ.” Then he walked thirty miles, lame as he was, to bring his wife, his daughter and two neighbours to be baptized.

That was the start of one of the great people movements in Christian history. The gospel spread from family to family through the poorest villages. In 1881 the census counted 3,912 Indian Christians in the Punjab. By 1911 there were 163,994. Not everyone welcomed it. Some missionaries worried that people were coming for the wrong reasons, or being baptized with too little teaching. Those were real questions. But Hyde saw in it what Paul saw in Corinth: God choosing “the weak things of the world.”

Hyde's home station was Ferozepore. By 1907 he was superintendent of the Moga circle, a district of 275 villages, working alongside an Indian evangelist named Jalal Masih. His mission's printed report for that year quotes his method:

“Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers. Then divide and go to the various parts of the town. Follow up inquirers and Christian converts in their places of work. Preach and baptize on the spot.”

He noticed that some people of higher caste were being drawn too, because, as he put it, “They see in Christians love not seen in their own.”

Hyde showed that love in ways nobody could miss. When village Christians arrived at a convention, he would embrace them “in Oriental style, laying his hand first on one shoulder and then on the other,” including Christians “of the lowest caste,” and he persuaded others to do the same. One witness thought this was his strong point: “Love won him victories.” He lived in village mud houses with his Indian evangelists, eating and sleeping alongside them. At the conventions it was often Gulla, the sweeper, who carried a plate of curry and rice to him. When Hyde died, his colleague wrote that he would be missed “by humble village preachers with whom he lived as a brother.”

In a society built on who could touch whom, a missionary hugging a low-caste villager in public was making a statement everyone understood.

Every school and town has its own caste system: who sits where, who gets noticed, who gets laughed at. The gospel ignores those lines. God has a habit of choosing exactly the people everyone else overlooks, and the Christians who serve them best don't just talk at them. They sit with them, eat with them, and treat them as family.

One thing to do this week: find one person who usually sits alone or gets left out, and sit with them, walk with them or eat with them. Don't turn them into a project. Just treat them like a brother or sister.

study_questions.question: Who was Ditt, and why does he matter to this story?
study_questions.answer: A lame hide-dealer from the lowest caste who was baptized around 1873, went home to his village, and brought his family and neighbours to Christ. The great people movement in the Punjab began with him.

study_questions.answer: “Begin the day in prayer and praise with your helpers.”

study_questions.question: How did Hyde show love across the caste lines of the Punjab?
study_questions.answer: He embraced low-caste Christians in public, lived and ate with his Indian evangelists in village houses, and was remembered as living with village preachers as a brother.

fields.title: The Man Who Never Sleeps
fields.body_html:
“And it came to pass in these days, that he went out into the mountain to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God.” — Luke 6:12 (ASV)

Somewhere in his middle years, the people of the Punjab gave Hyde a new name: “the man who never sleeps.” It wasn't literally true. He did sleep, though not much, and often in odd places. But at whatever hour of the night people passed his room, there seemed to be a light burning and a man on his knees.

How did it start? Not with a heroic resolution. Once, Hyde was due to give a Bible talk in the morning and hadn't had time to prepare, so he stayed up all night getting it ready. The talk went fine. Afterwards a thought came to him. He had spent a whole night preparing the message. What about preparing himself? “Would not a night of prayer and praise be a good preparation for a real blessing the following day?” So he tried it. He “enjoyed it so much that he repeated it the following night,” and others began to join him.

He never stopped preparing his talks carefully. But from then on he often said that “the preparation of the Messenger was quite as important as the preparation of the message.”

His friends describe a steady daily habit more than a heroic feat. One friend who shared a room with him found Hyde “on his knees long before I was up in the morning, though I was up with the dawn.” He would light the lamp several times in the night to read a passage of Scripture and pray. “His Bible was always in his hand,” that friend wrote, and “when he knelt to pray, the dear old Book was always open before him and his hands rested on it.”

In 1896, after four slow years, Hyde spoke to students at a conference in Lahore. He was honest about his own lack of fruit: “It may be, however, we have wanted results instead of wishing that needy souls might have life … Have we ever wept for souls? Have you? Have I?” That last question, “Have I?”, is a man still learning what he taught.

In the spring of 1904 Hyde was “one of the moving spirits” in a small group that started the Punjab Prayer Union. (Later books call him its founder; the early sources don't.) Members signed five questions. The first asked whether they were praying for new life in their own lives before anyone else's. The last was the practical heart of it:

“Will you set apart one-half hour each day as soon after noon as possible to pray for this awakening, and are you willing to pray till the awakening comes?”

That was it. Half an hour, not all night. A busy teacher could keep it. So could a village pastor. So could you. Its members believed that this ordinary promise, kept every day, was the hidden root of everything that happened next.

Hyde's friends were careful about one thing. He “dreaded lest any one should try to follow his example.” His all-night way of praying was his own, and, as you'll see, it cost him his health. Don't copy the form. But the idea that you need preparing, not just your homework or your performance, is for everyone. And a small promise kept daily can outlast a big resolution made once.

One thing to do this week: choose a fixed time every day this week, fifteen minutes or half an hour, whatever is honest, to pray with your Bible open in front of you. Same time each day. Keep the promise small enough that you can actually keep it.

study_questions.question: How did Hyde's nights of prayer begin?
study_questions.answer: After he stayed up all night preparing a Bible talk, he realised he had prepared the message but not himself, and spent the next night in prayer instead.

study_questions.question: What did Hyde mean by “the preparation of the Messenger”?
study_questions.answer: That the person speaking for God needs to be made ready before God just as much as the talk does.

study_questions.question: What did the Punjab Prayer Union ask its members to do each day?
study_questions.answer: To set apart half an hour, as soon after noon as possible, to pray for spiritual awakening, and to keep praying until it came.

fields.title: He Has Given Me No Message
fields.body_html:
“But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall bear witness of me: and ye also bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.” — John 15:26-27 (ASV)

In the late summer of 1904, missionaries and Indian Christian workers gathered at Sialkot for a new kind of meeting, a convention “for the deepening of the spiritual life.” Sialkot was not Hyde's station. It belonged to another Presbyterian mission, and he came each year as a guest. The convention still meets today, in Pakistan.

Hyde came to lead Bible studies. But what people remembered from that first year was an evening when he turned up late to a men's meeting. They had sung hymn after hymn. At last he came in, sat down on the mat in front of them, and was silent for a long time. Then he stood up:

“Brothers, I did not sleep any last night and I have not eaten anything to-day. I have been having a great controversy with God. I feel that he has wanted me to come here and testify to you concerning some things that he has done for me, and I have been arguing with him that I should not do this.”

His argument with God had been about one thing: whether to be honest in public about his own struggles. He spoke quietly for fifteen or twenty minutes about “some of the desperate conflicts that he had had with sin and how God had given him victory.” Then he sat down and said, “Let us have a season of prayer.” Man after man stood up to pray and confess. The leader's honesty opened the door for everyone else's. At the end of that convention Hyde said, “Oh, I must not lose this blessing.” His colleague added, “he never did lose it.”

The 1905 convention, from 25 August to 3 September, is the one everyone remembered. Nearly three hundred people came, most of them Indian workers. According to his friends' memoirs, Hyde was given the morning Bible readings on the Holy Spirit. His point was simple. The Holy Spirit is the real witness to Jesus; we only witness behind him. Then he turned it on the pastors:

“Is the Holy Spirit first in your pulpits, pastors? Do you consciously put him in front and keep yourselves behind him, when preaching?”

On the second morning, the mission's own official report says, the appointed speaker came in and said quietly, “I thank God, He has given me no message for you to-day.” Some faces showed surprise. The chairman moved aside and said, “The Holy Ghost is leader of this meeting.” The report doesn't name the speaker, but the memoirs tell the same story about Hyde, so it was almost certainly him.

Days of deep conviction, open confession and then joy followed. A room was set aside for prayer, and after the first day or two it was never empty, day or night. At one point Hyde felt God telling him to do something. He went and obeyed, but came back weeping because he had obeyed unwillingly: “Pray for me, brethren, that I may do this joyfully.”

Think about how hard that second morning was. Three hundred people were waiting, and he had nothing to say, so he said so and sat down. The young man who once wanted to shine could never have done it. Whether you're leading a small group, playing in a band, or just telling a friend about your faith, his question still stands: is the Holy Spirit first, or are you?

One thing to do this week: before the next thing you lead, play or speak at, pray one honest sentence: “Holy Spirit, go in front; I'll stay behind you.” Afterwards, notice whether you cared more about how you came across or about what God did.

study_questions.answer: Whether he should testify openly about his own struggles with sin. He finally obeyed, and his honesty led many other men to pray and confess.

study_questions.answer: Whether the Holy Spirit was first in their pulpits, and whether they consciously put him in front and kept themselves behind him when preaching.

study_questions.question: What happened when the appointed speaker had “no message”?
study_questions.answer: The chairman moved aside and declared that the Holy Ghost was leader of the meeting, and each morning meeting was left in the Spirit's hands.

fields.title: That Is My Work
fields.body_html:
“I am Jehovah thy God, Who brought thee up out of the land of Egypt: Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” — Psalm 81:10 (ASV)

Pengwern Jones, a Welsh missionary, first met Hyde in about 1906 at a mission meeting in Ludhiana. Jones had travelled all night by train and was due to give a talk at four o'clock. Over tea, Hyde said only, “I want to see you, I shall wait for you at the door.” He was waiting. “Come with me to the Prayer Room,” he said, “we want you there.”

Jones protested that he was tired and had a talk to give. He went anyway. Hyde lay face down on the floor. People prayed, came and went; meals were forgotten, and so were Jones's tiredness and nerves. At half past three Hyde got up and took Jones for a cup of tea, refusing any for himself. At the door of the hall he took his hand:

“Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work. When the service is over, come into the Prayer Room again and we shall praise God together.”

That explains the prayer room better than anything. Hyde didn't think praying was holier than preaching. They were two halves of one job, and his half was the hidden one.

At the Sialkot conventions there were prayer rooms for men and for women, where prayer went on day and night. Jones believed it was Hyde who “spent the first nights on the watch-tower.” One missionary attending for the first time complained that the leaders should be on the platform, not hiding in a back room. Two days later he came back beaming: “I have found out the secret of this Convention — it is that Prayer Room.”

Hyde's favourite way to pray was face down on the carpet. He would say a request, wait, and say it again, many times. Jones remembered him praying the verse at the top of this chapter, repeating one word “scores of times with long pauses between”: “'Wide, Lord.' 'Wide.' 'Open wide.' 'Wide.'” In the psalm, God's sadness is that his people wouldn't open their mouths to receive what he wanted to give. Hyde was asking God to stretch their expectations.

Don't picture it as gloomy. When someone found peace with God, Hyde would start to sing, and Jones describes him so full of joy that “he claps his hands and then his feet begin to move, and look, he begins to dance for joy and others join him.” A shy, deaf, once-gloomy Presbyterian, dancing on a carpet in a church in the Punjab.

There's a warning in here too. Hyde rarely came to meals, and his bed at the convention was never used. The lad of about sixteen who looked after him would cry “because he would not eat properly and would not go to bed to sleep.” But it wasn't a rule for him. When the lunch bell rang one day, a friend heard him whisper, “Father, is it thy will that I go?” There was a pause. Then “Thank you, Father,” and he got up with a smile and went to lunch.

Every church, team or friendship group needs someone doing the hidden work. You might never be the one on stage. You could be the one praying for whoever is.

One thing to do this week: pick one person facing something hard this week: a friend with an exam, a youth leader, a brother or sister. Tell them, “That's your work; praying for you is mine.” Then actually pray for them at that time.

study_questions.question: What did Hyde tell Jones at the door of the hall?
study_questions.answer: “Go in and speak, that is your work. I shall go back to the Prayer Room to pray for you, that is my work.”

study_questions.question: Why did Hyde keep repeating the word “wide”?
study_questions.answer: He was praying Psalm 81:10, “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it,” asking God to enlarge his people's expectation so they would receive what God was ready to give.

study_questions.question: How do we know Hyde did not treat skipping meals as a rule?
study_questions.answer: When the lunch bell rang he asked, “Father, is it thy will that I go?” and then thanked God and went to lunch.

fields.title: What About That One?
fields.body_html:
“What man of you, having a hundred sheep, and having lost one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?” — Luke 15:4 (ASV)

In the summer of 1908 Hyde went to the hills to escape the heat and pray. His host, very probably his close friend McCheyne Paterson, saw that he was “bowed down with sore travail of soul.” He missed meals. Paterson would find him “lying as in great agony, or walking up and down as if an inward fire were burning in his bones.” Day after day they heard him pleading for the people of his district, with sobs: “Father, give me these souls or I die!” (Later books word it differently; this is how the earliest one records it.) It echoes Rachel in Genesis, longing for a child: “Give me children, or else I die.”

Now for the most famous claim about Hyde, which needs care. fields.title: Show Me What Is Lovely
fields.body_html:
“for he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye.” — Zechariah 2:8 (ASV)

The story about Hyde that may have done the most good is the one that shows him at his worst. Around 1910 he was burdened about an Indian pastor whose spiritual life seemed to have gone cold, and whose congregation had gone cold with him. So Hyde went into his room to pray for him. He began, “O Father, thou knowest how cold —“

He never finished the sentence. In his friends' telling, it was as if a hand had been laid on his lips, and a voice said to him sternly: “He that toucheth him, toucheth the apple of mine eye.” Hyde was horrified. He cried out, “Forgive me, Father, in that I have been an accuser of the brethren before thee!”

“The accuser of the brethren” is one of the Bible's names for Satan. Hyde had come to do the work of someone who prays for others, and found he had been doing the devil's work instead. It's a trap for people who pray. We bring someone to God out of concern, and before we know it we're listing their faults.

Then Hyde did the important thing. He confessed it, and he remembered Philippians 4:8: “whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report … think on these things.” So he prayed a new prayer: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother's life.” The answer came “like a flash.” The pastor had given up everything for Christ and had suffered for it at the hands of his own relatives. He had worked hard for years, handled a difficult congregation with tact, healed many quarrels, and was a good husband. Hyde spent his whole time of prayer thanking God for him. “He could not recall a single petition,” his friend wrote, “nothing but thanksgiving!”

When Hyde went back down from the hills, he heard that the pastor had just received a great spiritual uplift, at about the time Hyde had been praising God for him. “While he was praising, God was blessing.” That isn't a formula that forces God's hand, and Hyde wouldn't have claimed one. But criticism sees people as problems. Thanksgiving sees them as God's work in progress.

Praise ran all through Hyde's life. One morning, touring the villages, he woke with a headache so bad he couldn't lift his head. He couldn't preach. But he thanked God “for the love that had permitted that headache,” and had his bed carried into the shade. The village women, who had never come forward although some of their husbands had been baptized, came to sympathise with the sick missionary. He talked with them about Christ, and they decided there and then to be baptized. His circle of friends had a phrase for this kind of thing: “Praising God through shut teeth.”

Listen to how you talk about people who annoy you, even in your prayers. Does it sound more like praying for them or like a list of charges against them? A close friend of Hyde's said he “never heard him criticizing any persons, though he could vehemently denounce sin.” This doesn't mean pretending wrong things are fine. It means any correcting starts from thankfulness.

One thing to do this week: pick the person who irritates you most right now and pray Hyde's prayer about them by name: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report” in their life. Write down three things. Then thank God for each one, without adding a “but.”

study_questions.answer: “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother's life.” He ended up spending the whole time thanking God for the pastor.

study_questions.answer: Too ill to preach, Hyde thanked God for it and lay in the shade. The village women came to sympathise, he spoke with them about Christ, and they decided to be baptized.

fields.title: Tears at a Train Window
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore watch ye, remembering that by the space of three years I ceased not to admonish every one night and day with tears.” — Acts 20:31 (ASV)

Most of the people Hyde led to Christ have no names in the records. One is known by his initials, J. N. He was a young Brahman, from the highest Hindu caste, who had gone to a mission school. When he started work he publicly confessed Christ, in the face of “the bitterest opposition” of his widowed mother and his relatives. Then his family changed tactics and started being kind to him. He went home, fell in with young men who led him into drink, and denied his Lord.

He was miserable, and he went to Hyde, “who received him as did the father his prodigal son.” He came to live with Hyde and came back to faith. Then the drink took hold of him again, and again. More than once he stole Hyde's clothes and sold them to buy liquor. Hyde told a friend with a smile, “I may not get up to you to the hills this summer, the Father evidently desires me to spend my hot weather in the plains, for I have no warm clothes left!”

One day a Christian woman working as a ticket collector at a railway station saw a missionary talking to a young man sitting in a train bound for Lahore. The young man was loud and almost abusive: “I am tired of this sort of thing. I am going to my boon companions and shall have a good time.” The missionary leaned into the carriage window, pleading with him in Christ's name, with tears running down his cheeks. The young man wouldn't listen. The train pulled out.

The next day she saw the same young man coming back. He looked up at her with a pale face. “I am going back to him,” he said. “I have not been able to sleep all night — I could not forget his tears.” He found Hyde in his room, praying. Hyde took him in his arms and said, “I have just been praying that God would send you back to me, and see, He has answered me!”

Another time, after J. N. had walked for two days to find him, Hyde made him lie down and rubbed his swollen feet. A Brahman did not expect a European missionary to touch his feet. Years later J. N. said, “I often see him in my dreams before me as of old.”

Hyde's patience drove some people mad. One cold night he knocked at an Indian evangelist's door to borrow a sheet. The evangelist snapped through the closed door that the drunk who had been staying with Hyde had run off with his blankets, and that Hyde put everyone out by doing things like this. Hyde's answer: “If the prodigal had come back to you, you would have taken a stick to him!”

Here's the honest part. J. N.'s story doesn't end neatly. About ten years after Hyde died, he was “much chastened,” but he still hadn't given up drink. That's where the record stops. Hyde's tears didn't end J. N.'s struggle. They kept him coming back.

Love doesn't always fix people, and fixing people isn't your job. But somebody in your life may need to see that you care about them more than about your pride. If someone you love is caught by drink, drugs or anything else that is taking them over, you don't have to carry it alone: talk to a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a helpline where you live. And if you're the one who keeps falling back, keep coming back. That's what J. N. did.

One thing to do this week: think of one person who has drifted away from God or from you. Send them a message this week with no lecture in it, just that you care about them and are praying for them. Then pray for them.

study_questions.answer: “If the prodigal had come back to you, you would have taken a stick to him!” He chose to act like the father in the parable, not the angry elder brother.

study_questions.answer: It is honest. Ten years after Hyde's death J. N. was still struggling with drink. Hyde's love didn't fix him, but it kept him coming back.

fields.title: A Heart on the Wrong Side
fields.body_html:
“And he saith unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while. For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.” — Mark 6:31 (ASV)

The Sialkot convention of 1910 was Hyde's last. His friends said “the long sleepless nights and weary days of watching with prayer” were “written on every feature of his face.” Afterwards he went to Calcutta to lead meetings and stayed with a friend. He had a fever the whole time but led every meeting. At night the friend, lying awake across the passage, watched Hyde's light come on at twelve, at two, at four and at five.

The friend persuaded him to see a doctor. As the friend remembered it, the doctor said:

“The heart is in an awful condition. I have never come across such a bad case as this. It has been shifted out of its natural position on the left side to a place over on the right side. Through stress and strain it is in such a bad condition that it will require months and months of strictly quiet life to bring it back again to anything like its normal state. What have you been doing with yourself?”

Hyde said nothing. He only smiled. His friend was sure he knew the cause: years of praying day and night.

This is where the famous claim comes from, that prayer physically moved Hyde's heart across his chest. Be careful with it. What we have is a friend's memory, written down years later, of one doctor's remark. We don't know the doctor's name or have his notes, and the doctor himself didn't claim to know the cause; he asked. A heart on the right side has known medical explanations: some people are born that way, and disease in the chest can push a heart over. Within eighteen months Hyde died of a malignant tumour, and he had suffered bad headaches for years. Nobody can diagnose him a century later. The honest course is to tell the story as his friends told it and leave the miracle unclaimed.

That doesn't mean his way of life did him no harm. It almost certainly did. Years of little sleep, missed meals and long vigils while feverish wear a body down. One missionary said Hyde had laid down his life “calmly and deliberately for the Church of God in India.” But Hyde's colleague also recorded that some criticised the way he “seemed to deny to the flesh even its just claims.” Those last words matter: just claims. Your body's needs are real. The teenage helper who cried because his master wouldn't eat or sleep wasn't less spiritual than Hyde. He was seeing clearly.

When the apostles were too busy even to eat, Jesus didn't tell them to pray harder. He told them to come away and rest. When the prophet Elijah collapsed in despair, an angel told him, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for thee.” Hyde's friends urged people to follow his spirit of prayer, “but not necessarily in the 'form' that he manifested it.”

Hyde didn't take the months of quiet the doctor ordered. In March 1911 he left India for the last time, as an early biographer put it, a “dying man.”

Some of us are more at risk of giving God too little. Some are the other kind: running on no sleep, skipping meals, pushing harder and calling it devotion or discipline. Rest, food and sleep are gifts from God, not signs of weakness. If you aren't eating or sleeping properly, or you feel you have to punish your body to be good enough, please tell a safe person: a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

One thing to do this week: protect your sleep. Choose a time to put your phone away each night and keep to it for seven days. When you lie down, thank God for sleep as his gift.

study_questions.answer: As a friend remembered it, the doctor said the heart was in an awful condition and had shifted from the left side to the right, and he asked Hyde what he had been doing to himself.

study_questions.question: Why does the book refuse to claim that prayer moved Hyde's heart?
study_questions.answer: Because the story is one friend's later memory of one examination, the doctor didn't know the cause, and a heart on the right side has known medical explanations, including illness like the tumour that later killed him.

study_questions.question: What does “its just claims” teach about the body?
study_questions.answer: That the body's needs for food, sleep and rest are real and right, and that neglecting them is not automatically more spiritual.

fields.title: Victory, Victory, Victory
fields.body_html:
“but thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” — 1 Corinthians 15:57 (ASV)

On Good Friday, 14 April 1911, Hyde's ship reached Liverpool, and he went to stay with Pengwern Jones in Llangollen, Wales. They walked the hills and prayed together. There they visited an elderly woman who was very deaf and complained that she couldn't hear anything at church. “You ought to praise God for that,” Hyde told her. He couldn't hear either, he explained, so he would look at the preacher and pray for him, and then look at the people one by one and pray for each. The deafness he had carried for twenty years had become a gift he could pass on. She wrote later that his advice had made a wonderful difference to her life.

Then he heard that the American evangelist J. Wilbur Chapman was struggling with a mission at Shrewsbury, in England. Hardly anyone came, and some local ministers treated it “as some little side-show.” Hyde was a stranger and seriously ill, but he said, “I cannot leave a brother minister to bear this burden alone,” and came back for a week to pray. Chapman later wrote that “instantly the tide turned in our work,” and his biographer records that at least fifty people responded that day. Before Chapman left, he asked Hyde to pray for him, and remembered the prayer like this:

“My Father, here is a minister who sorely needs Thy help, do bless him, I beseech Thee, may his life be precious in Thy sight.”

A more dramatic version of that scene, with a locked door and long silences, comes from an undated letter. The account Chapman published himself is the quieter one. Either way, the week cost Hyde dearly. He “crawled back” to Jones's house, so weak he could hardly speak, and whispered: “The burden was very heavy, but my dear Saviour's burden for me took Him down to the grave.”

That spring someone started singing a hymn in the middle of his talk, and the message was never given. Another time he travelled a long way while ill and was never even invited to speak. He didn't complain. Of unkindness he said, “This is my cross which He wants me to take up and carry for Him.”

In August he sailed for America. Doctors at Clifton Springs, New York, found a malignant tumour and operated. He wrote to his sister: “Am still in bed or wheel chair getting a fine rest and doing a lot of the ministry of intercession, and having not a few opportunities of personal work.” In December he moved to her home in Northampton, Massachusetts. The tumour returned, and his last weeks were “days of unutterable suffering.” Yet in the middle of it he said, “Thank God for pain, thank God for everything!” To his sister he said, “It's just victory, victory, victory.”

John Hyde died at Northampton on 17 February 1912, aged forty-six. (Many books say he died at Clifton Springs, but that is only where he was treated.)
